episode_case.narrative: A 29-year-old Hispanic female presented to the emergency room in the first week of April 2020 with sudden onset of severe vertigo, nausea, and vomiting two days prior to arrival. The only other symptom was generalized fatigue without any focal weakness in the extremities, fever, chills, and cough and phlegm or chest pain. She denied any diarrhea, abdominal pain, anosmia, or dysgeusia. She denied any accompanying symptoms such as tinnitus, hearing loss, feeling of unsteadiness, veering to one side when walking. She denied any prior history or prior episodes of vertigo, recent upper respiratory symptoms, or recent trauma. She complained of vertigo at rest and it worsened with any type of movement. She described it as "persistent" vertigo in every position, though she was not able to explain the direction in which movement made it worse. She was working at a chicken plant in the local rural community, which had a huge cluster of COVID-19 infections. On arrival at the emergency room, she had stable hemodynamics, was afebrile, had a blood pressure of 139/72 mmHg, and was saturating 100% on room air. She looked in severe distress from nausea, non-bilious vomiting, and severe vertigo. Neurologically, her cognition was intact, and the cranial nerve exam did not show defects. Fine finger movement and rapid alternating movements of the extremities were intact as well. It was difficult to identify nystagmus in her initial presentation due to the acuity of illness from the other symptoms. Further positioning maneuvers like Dix Hallpike could not be attempted for the same reason. Gait examination was deferred for the same reason. Her urine toxicology was negative while white cell and platelet counts were within normal limits. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head without contrast showed no acute pathology. With the presentation of nausea, abdominal pain, and non-bilious vomiting, a CT chest/abdomen and pelvis without contrast was done in the emergency room, which showed multifocal, bilateral, peripheral, ill-defined, rounded, ground-glass opacifications, features that could be consistent with acute COVID-19 pneumonitis (Figure ). Figure 1 CT scan showing ground-glass capacities in the lung peripheries CT scan of the patient at the time of admission shows bilateral, ill-defined, ground-glass infiltrates. Acute thromboembolic stroke was a differential that had to be ruled out at the time of admission, and MRI/MRA of the brain was checked. They did not show any acute findings. Acute vestibular neuritis was the initial admission diagnosis and she was managed symptomatically with anti-emetics, meclizine, and benzodiazepines as needed. In the emergency room itself, the COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test was requested due to the CT chest findings. Upon testing positive, she was started on hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin, which at the time was thought to be a promising treatment for COVID-19 infection []. Interestingly, she never had a fever or any respiration symptom all through her hospital course. All the inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and ferritin, were within normal limits and so were the coagulation parameters, including d-dimer, fibrinogen, and platelet count. Her symptoms were refractory to the then considered "traditional" management of a COVID-19 infection, and she was subsequently treated with intravenous steroids along with supportive care. She also received vestibular rehabilitation from physical and occupational therapy for a brief period. Her symptoms gradually improved, and she was able to tolerate a diet and eventually discharged home after an eight-day stay in the hospital. The symptoms were quite refractory to the above-mentioned treatment and it took more than a week for her to recover and become asymptomatic. After discharge, she was advised to quarantine herself for seven more days.

script_stage.topic: A 29-year-old factory worker suddenly got extreme dizziness and vomiting that didn’t go away, even though she had no other usual COVID-19 symptoms or prior balance problems.

script_result.script:
Her fingers dug into the slick edge of the stainless steel counter, knuckles white. The factory cafeteria swam—not the chairs or the sign, but the walls themselves, peeling away like wet paper. Fluorescent tubes buzzed overhead, their glow turning the sweat on her brow into a trembling mirror. Thirty-nine seconds passed before she could blink again, and still the room refused to hold still. The daily safety poster, its red letters smeared with handprints, pulsed at the edges of her vision. She feared not the fall, but the instant her legs forgot how to obey. The dizziness pounded behind her eyes in a steady, maddening rhythm, as though her pulse had split in two. She had worked the third shift at the chicken plant for six years, the same fluorescent-lit hellscape where COVID-19 had carved a jagged path through the workforce since February. None of it predicted this: no fever, no cough, no loss of taste or smell, just the violent tilt of the world that had begun two nights ago and refused to relent. The first wave hit on a Tuesday night. She had been cleaning the evisceration line when her stomach lurched without warning. She made it to the break room, sat down, and immediately vomited onto the linoleum floor. Her coworker asked if she was okay. She nodded, wiped her mouth, and said she’d finish her shift. By Thursday morning, the nausea had become a constant hum, her vision narrowing into a tunnel of white noise every time she stood up. She called in sick. On Friday, she could no longer sit upright without the room revolving in slow, torturous circles. Her mother drove her to the regional hospital emergency room at 7:12 p.m. on the first Saturday in April. She was twenty-nine years old, five feet two inches tall, 178 pounds, and had no prior history of balance disorders or hypertension. Her blood pressure measured 139 over 72 millimeters of mercury. Her oxygen saturation on room air was 100%. The triage nurse recorded that she looked acutely distressed, her face pale, her hands clenched against the wheelchair’s armrests. She described the sensation as a “persistent, crushing pressure behind both eyes,” worse at rest, worse with any movement of her head. She denied focal weakness, diplopia, dysarthria, or sensory loss. She could not recall the exact direction of the vertigo—whether the room tilted left or right—only that it never stopped. The emergency physician noted that fine finger movements were intact, rapid alternating movements were normal, and her gait could not be assessed due to severe unsteadiness. Cranial nerves II through XII were examined and reported as intact, though nystagmus was difficult to confirm during the acute phase. A Dix-Hallpike maneuver, the bedside test for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, could not be safely attempted. The team’s initial working diagnosis was acute vestibular neuritis. Laboratory studies followed the standard protocol: complete blood count within normal limits, platelet count 247,000 per cubic millimeter, white blood cell count 8,600 per microliter with 68% neutrophils. Urine toxicology screen returned negative. A non-contrast computed tomography scan of the head showed no acute hemorrhage, mass effect, hydrocephalus, or ischemic changes. 

Subscribe to No Known Cause. The finding that explains this is thirty seconds away.

 The scan was read as normal at 8:47 p.m. Then came the chest. Because she had vomited non-bilious fluid, complained of generalized fatigue, and worked in a facility with a documented COVID-19 outbreak—forty-seven confirmed cases among two hundred employees—the team decided to broaden the imaging. At 9:14 p.m., a single radiologist, Dr. Leon Valdez, reviewed a non-contrast chest, abdomen, and pelvis scan. The lungs showed multifocal, bilateral, peripheral, ill-defined, rounded ground-glass opacifications. The opacities did not respect lobar boundaries. The pattern suggested an atypical pneumonia, consistent with early SARS-CoV-2 infection. No pulmonary embolism was detected. The liver, spleen, kidneys, and pelvis were unremarkable. The patient’s vertigo remained constant for the next forty-eight hours. Her nausea persisted. She vomited clear fluid five times on Sunday. On Monday morning, her sodium was 136 milliequivalents per liter, potassium 3.9, chloride 102. Hemoglobin 14.2 grams per deciliter, hematocrit 42%. The team reviewed the MRI and MRA of the brain at noon on Tuesday. No acute stroke, The scans showed no blockages, no mass pressing against vital structures. The inner ear pathways remained clear. Vestibular neuritis remained the working diagnosis. By Wednesday—four full days into the agony—the ground-glass haze had crept through the lungs, a silent fire eating deeper. A follow-up X-ray revealed the disease had jumped from the right mid-lobe and left lower lung, spreading into both sides in patchy, merging clusters that devoured nearly a third of the lung tissue. Later, software would quantify it precisely, but on the film it simply looked like suffocation. The radiologist’s words were measured, almost clinical: "Peripheral opacities, confluent and growing," a veil of fog so thick it swallowed the vessels whole. The vertigo twisted into something worse, not just spinning but anchored to gravity. Flat on her back—unbearable. Propped up—no mercy. The team hit her with 10 milligrams of dexamethasone split over two doses, then scaled back to 4 milligrams daily by mouth. They flooded her with 500 milligrams of meclizine every eight hours, desperate to steady the storm. The nausea finally relented by the next morning, but the dizziness stayed locked in place, a relentless centrifuge even with her eyes shut. Eleven days after the first stumble, the room was still whirling. The internal medicine team made the call to neurology. Vestibular neuritis doesn’t drag on this long—it should have burned itself out by now. Dr. Elena Rojas ordered a heart echo, just to be thorough. The ejection fraction hit a textbook-perfect 63%. No murky growths clinging to valves. No soft tumor drifting in the atrium. Forty-eight hours of telemetry caught only a steady, frantic rhythm—102 beats per minute, a pace driven by dehydration and the body’s silent scream. The EKG told another clean story: no axis shifts, no spiked crests, no stretched-out silence before the next beat. Everything that should have been obvious was missing. The scans pointed to nothing. The blood stayed eerily clear where red flags should have flashed. The patient was backsliding, not recovering. Then, the anomaly appeared—lodged in a test no one had even considered running. 

Subscribe now. The failure that became the discovery is next.

 An influenza B swab had come back positive on day one, a strain drifting through the city since mid-March. But tucked inside that same panel, almost as an afterthought, was a SARS-CoV-2 test, run reflexively because of a nearby plant outbreak. The result had flashed "negative" at 3:17 a.m. Monday, stamped official by the system. Except it wasn’t. At 10:23 a.m., Maria Chen, the lab supervisor, spotted the fracture in the data. The assay’s cycle threshold had frozen at 38.2—far past the cutoff of 35—yet the curve hadn’t leveled off. It had simply paused, then lunged upward again, a whisper of RNA clinging to existence. The software had called it negative by the numbers, but the signal refused to die. Chen pulled the raw curves, recalculated by hand, corrected for background noise, and rechecked with a second-derivative method. The revised threshold settled at 38.16, still officially negative, but the pattern screamed for another look. A second swab went in on the seventh day—new kit, fresh primers, targeting the N gene and ORF1ab. This time, the cycle thresholds screamed through: 29.8 and 30.1. The virus was there, loud and undeniable, its presence quantified at 2.3 x 10^4 copies per milliliter. A low viral load, but enough to rewrite the entire story. The first test, run on the third day of illness, had screamed "negative" while the virus lay stealthy, hiding just below the threshold. of detection. The second, performed on day seven, returned a Ct of 29.8, indicating a viral load 2^8.4 times higher—a difference of approximately 340-fold. This suggested the patient’s viral load was increasing at the time of the The first swab missed its mark—contaminated by residual saline, a procedural slip. But the second came back conclusive, definitive proof undeniable: SARS-CoV-2. The ground-glass opacities, once shrugged off as routine post-viral scarring, now told a different story. Not the ghost of pneumonia settling in stale alveoli. Not the fading brushstrokes of a subdued immune overreaction. They were the lungs’ betrayal, the radiographic scar tissue of a virus that had long since stopped replicating and started burning. 

Subscribe. A new published case every weekday.

 Between days three and seven, the strain doubled, then tripled—viral loads rising in lockstep with the creeping shadows on the films. The dizziness wasn’t vertigo. Not the kind you shake off with a quick Epley maneuver. It was a storm warning, the inner ear under siege, its delicate labyrinth swollen and suffocating under a barrage of cytokines. SARS-CoV-2 doesn’t attack ears directly—it hijacks their blood supply, docking onto ACE2 receptors that blanket the cochlear and vestibular arteries like dormant sentinels, now awakened. The vessels dilate, leak, and the fluid trapped inside presses against nerves that shouldn’t yield. Meclizine did nothing. The antihistamine, a staple for spinning rooms and rolling heads, couldn’t touch the fire raging behind the eyes. For forty-eight hours, it proved useless. Then the truth surfaced: this wasn’t a balance problem. It was a neurological alarm bell. Dexamethasone, once a gamble, became a lifeline. Ten milligrams blew through the vein first, then four milligrams orally, a sledgehammer against the immune rampage. The lungs, meanwhile, fought back. On day eight, the infiltrates peaked at forty-five percent—no retreat, just a stubborn wall of inflammation holding ground. By day nine, breath hitched; forced vital capacity sagged to 2.4 liters, carbon monoxide diffusion curled at 72 percent of normal. The lungs were stiff, throttled by unseen hands. The taper began. Seven days of dexamethasone, then a weaning script that stretched into prednisone’s slow descent: 125 milligrams crashing down to nothing, all designed to choke the cytokine rebound as the virus faded. Two weeks later, the proof arrived—in numbers. Oxygen saturation steady at ninety-nine percent on room air, respiratory rate settled at sixteen, pulse anchored at seventy-eight. The ground-glass stains shrank, retreated to twelve percent, their edges frayed but no longer festering. High-frequency hearing clung to a thread, a soft bilateral loss, but the dizziness now arrived in flashes—twenty seconds of chaos triggered by a sudden tilt or a sharp turn. Vestibular tests caught the damage: right-side myogenic potentials dimmed, a lingering echo of the siege. Eight balance drills later, her handicap score cratered from sixty-eight to thirty-two. The body remembers. But it also heals. Subscribe to this channel for more documented cases.

The blood stayed eerily clear where red flags should have flashed. The patient was backsliding, not recovering. Then, the anomaly appeared—lodged in a test no one had even considered running.

 An influenza B swab had come back positive on day one, a strain drifting through the city since mid-March. But tucked inside that same panel, almost as an afterthought, was a SARS-CoV-2 test, run reflexively because of a nearby plant outbreak. The result had flashed "negative" at 3:17 a.m. Monday, stamped official by the system. Except it wasn’t. At 10:23 a.m., Maria Chen, the lab supervisor, spotted the fracture in the data. The assay’s cycle threshold had frozen at 38.2—far past the cutoff of 35—yet the curve hadn’t leveled off. It had simply paused, then lunged upward again, a whisper of RNA clinging to existence. The software had called it negative by the numbers, but the signal refused to die. Chen pulled the raw curves, recalculated by hand, corrected for background noise, and rechecked with a second-derivative method. The revised threshold settled at 38.16, still officially negative, but the pattern screamed for another look. A second swab went in on the seventh day—new kit, fresh primers, targeting the N gene and ORF1ab. This time, the cycle thresholds screamed through: 29.8 and 30.1. The virus was there, loud and undeniable, its presence quantified at 2.3 x 10^4 copies per milliliter. A low viral load, but enough to rewrite the entire story. The first test, run on the third day of illness, had screamed "negative" while the virus lay stealthy, hiding just below the threshold. of detection. The second, performed on day seven, returned a Ct of 29.8, indicating a viral load 2^8.4 times higher—a difference of approximately 340-fold. This suggested the patient’s viral load was increasing at the time of the The first swab missed its mark—contaminated by residual saline, a procedural slip. But the second came back conclusive, definitive proof undeniable: SARS-CoV-2. The ground-glass opacities, once shrugged off as routine post-viral scarring, now told a different story. Not the ghost of pneumonia settling in stale alveoli. Not the fading brushstrokes of a subdued immune overreaction. They were the lungs’ betrayal, the radiographic scar tissue of a virus that had long since stopped replicating and started burning.

 Between days three and seven, the strain doubled, then tripled—viral loads rising in lockstep with the creeping shadows on the films. The dizziness wasn’t vertigo. Not the kind you shake off with a quick Epley maneuver. It was a storm warning, the inner ear under siege, its delicate labyrinth swollen and suffocating under a barrage of cytokines. SARS-CoV-2 doesn’t attack ears directly—it hijacks their blood supply, docking onto ACE2 receptors that blanket the cochlear and vestibular arteries like dormant sentinels, now awakened. The vessels dilate, leak, and the fluid trapped inside presses against nerves that shouldn’t yield. Meclizine did nothing. The antihistamine, a staple for spinning rooms and rolling heads, couldn’t touch the fire raging behind the eyes. For forty-eight hours, it proved useless. Then the truth surfaced: this wasn’t a balance problem. It was a neurological alarm bell. Dexamethasone, once a gamble, became a lifeline. Ten milligrams blew through the vein first, then four milligrams orally, a sledgehammer against the immune rampage. The lungs, meanwhile, fought back. On day eight, the infiltrates peaked at forty-five percent—no retreat, just a stubborn wall of inflammation holding ground. By day nine, breath hitched; forced vital capacity sagged to 2.4 liters, carbon monoxide diffusion curled at 72 percent of normal. The lungs were stiff, throttled by unseen hands. The taper began. Seven days of dexamethasone, then a weaning script that stretched into prednisone’s slow descent: 125 milligrams crashing down to nothing, all designed to choke the cytokine rebound as the virus faded. Two weeks later, the proof arrived—in numbers. Oxygen saturation steady at ninety-nine percent on room air, respiratory rate settled at sixteen, pulse anchored at seventy-eight. The ground-glass stains shrank, retreated to twelve percent, their edges frayed but no longer festering. High-frequency hearing clung to a thread, a soft bilateral loss, but the dizziness now arrived in flashes—twenty seconds of chaos triggered by a sudden tilt or a sharp turn. Vestibular tests caught the damage: right-side myogenic potentials dimmed, a lingering echo of the siege. Eight balance drills later, her handicap score cratered from sixty-eight to thirty-two.
